title: Rooting Success Metrics and Failure Diagnosis
objective: Define propagation success with multiple measurable endpoints and use failure patterns to identify the limiting step.

terms.definition: The proportion of started cuttings that meet a defined rooted criterion at a stated observation time.
Elapsed time from propagation start to a defined root-emergence or root-readiness endpoint.
A predefined assessment of root amount, distribution, condition, and functional readiness rather than presence alone.
The proportion of propagated plants remaining alive and meeting a stated viability criterion at a defined time.
The degree to which individuals in a batch cluster around the same measured developmental or performance state.
A data condition in which the exact event time is not observed for every individual, such as cuttings that have not rooted by the final observation.
A predefined classification used to group failed or rejected propagules by observable pattern or diagnostic stage.

coreScience: Rooting percentage alone can hide slow, weak, or highly variable batches. A complete assessment includes time to root, root number, length or mass, distribution, callus, shoot condition, transplant survival, and later uniformity.

Failure can occur before root initiation, during emergence, or after transplant. Basal rot, desiccation, heavy callus, delayed rooting, weak roots, sudden post-dome wilt, and uneven tray patterns point to different hypotheses.
Tray position and donor identity must be retained. Averages can conceal edge drying, light gradients, blocked irrigation, one contaminated mother, or an operator effect.
cultivationRelevance: Define acceptance criteria before the batch begins. Photograph representative successes and failures, retain rejects long enough for diagnosis when safe, and compare changes against a current standard.

measureAndRecord.requirement: Cuttings started; viable at each observation; first root date; rooting percentage; root score; callus/rot; spatial map; transplant survival; rejection reason; mother and operator effects.

For rooting success metrics and failure diagnosis, record the relevant developmental stage, environment, operator or treatment condition, and time sequence so the biological response can be separated from handling and facility effects.

Record the defined success endpoint, failures and off-types, replicate or batch variation, and any identity, health, rooting, survival, or follow-up test used to verify that the apparent result persisted after establishment.

misconceptions: Any visible root is a successful clone. Visible similarity alone does not prove equivalent physiological state, health status, or later performance; identity and outcome measurements answer different questions.

A high final rooting percentage means the protocol is efficient. A single observation or negative symptom check cannot exclude latent infection, developmental history, or protocol-specific effects; use the appropriate follow-up test or repeated observation.
All failures are caused by humidity. Cultivar names, appearance, and one successful batch are not substitutes for traceable identity, controlled comparison, and repeatable propagation outcomes.
evidenceLimits: Metrics and acceptance limits depend on intended use. Research-grade, nursery, clean-stock, and emergency-rescue programs may require different endpoints.
